title: Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers
one_liner: A neutral third party installs pre-construction sensors around proposed data centers and administers a developer-funded, automatic payout guarantee to neighbors, so permit fights run on evidence.
customer: Independent and mid-size data center developers seeking 50-500 MW campus approvals in contested counties. County commissions and state regulators are a second buyer because they can make the service a permit condition. Hyperscalers with in-house community teams are not the target.
problem: Permit fights are evidence-poor. Nobody has a pre-construction baseline of well levels, night-time noise, air quality or voltage at homes, so every later complaint about dry wells or a hum can be neither proven nor disproven. Both sides fight on feelings and lawyers. Politics has turned: New York paused environmental permits for data centers of 50 MW or more in July 2026, Texas ordered its environmental regulator to stop issuing new data center permits in September 2026, and local pauses now exist in at least 14 states. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found only 14% of Americans would welcome one nearby.
solution: Baseline-in-a-Box. Over 60-90 days before the application, deploy 30-60 low-cost sensors: property-line night noise, depth and conductivity in volunteer neighbors' wells, PM2.5, night-sky brightness, and voltage sag at homes. Publish a read-only public dashboard. Have a university extension hydrogeologist and an acoustician review the methods. Escrow the data with hash-anchored timestamps so neither side can edit it. Keep monitoring for 10 years. Then add a Neighbor Guarantee: a developer-funded escrow that pays affected households automatically, like parametric crop insurance, when verified well drawdown or noise exceedances occur. No lawsuit is needed.
why_now: In 2026 the moratorium movement jumped from town boards to governors' offices (New York's executive order of July 14, Texas's TCEQ permit halt of September 21). Developers now need social license as much as megawatts, and regulators are actively drafting the frameworks that will say what evidence counts.
revenue_model: The developer pays $75-150k per site for setup, $4-10k per month for monitoring, and an 8-10% administration fee on the guarantee escrow. Counties that write the service into permit conditions create repeat demand. Later, anonymized data licensing to regulators and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The baseline protects the developer more than the opponents. It is the only defense against future exaggerated or mistaken claims, and it turns 'trust us' into 'audit us'. Parametric payouts replace adversarial claims, which is why a rational developer buys it from a neutral party rather than opposing it.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a pending rezoning hearing (Georgia, Virginia, Indiana, Pennsylvania or Texas). Offer the developer's land agent a free 30-day pilot on 10 neighbor wells with an agricultural-extension partner. Build nodes from off-the-shelf parts at about $1.5-3k each. Present the live dashboard at the public hearing and convert that developer to a paid contract. Use the result as the case study for the next 5 developers.
